# Money supply, debasement and inflation (`quantity_theory_inflation`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/economy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Economy & finance (`economy`)
- Deps: helped by coinage, paper_money
- Core idea: If money circulates at the same speed and its quantity grows faster than the volume of transactions, the average transaction price rises. Written as MV = PT: money times the speed it changes hands equals price level times transactions. Debasement, new notes and silver inflows can expand the money supply, but output and the demand to hold money can also change. Unexpected inflation reduces the purchasing power of fixed payments and the real burden of fixed nominal debts. Compare England's Great Debasement with paper issues in revolutionary France.
- Pitfalls:
  - Blaming greedy merchants or hoarders for a general price rise caused by the mint or the printing house
  - Believing more money makes a country richer: Spain imported vast silver and suffered inflation while productive neighbours gained
  - Thinking the relation is exact and immediate: velocity changes with confidence, and if output grows, more money need not raise prices
  - Fighting inflation with price ceilings: shortages and black markets follow
  - Forgetting the opposite danger: a shortage of money (deflation) strangles trade and ruins debtors
- History: china: c. 4th–1st c. BC – the Guanzi discusses how the quantity of money and grain the state holds moves prices; 1077 Shen Kuo contrasts coins hoarded in one household with the same coins passing repeatedly among ten households; rome: 3rd c. AD – the silver content of the coinage falls to a few per cent and prices rise many times over; 301 Diocletian answers with price controls that fail; islamic: 1405 – al-Maqrizi (Ighathat al-umma) blames Egypt's price rise on excessive issue of copper coin; europe: c. 1355–1360 – Nicole Oresme, De moneta, against debasement; 1526 Copernicus' treatise on coinage; 1556 Azpilcueta and 1568 Bodin link the price rise to American silver; 1752 Hume, Of Money; 1911 Irving Fisher's equation of exchange; 1923 German hyperinflation; americas: 1545 onwards – Potosí silver feeds a century-long rise in European and Asian prices (the role of population growth is disputed)
- Read:
  - Li Tao, Xu Zizhi tongjian changbian (12th c.), juan 283, recording Shen Kuo’s monetary proposals
  - Jean Bodin, Response to the Paradoxes of Malestroit (1568)
  - Irving Fisher, The Purchasing Power of Money (1911)
  - Milton Friedman & Anna J. Schwartz, A Monetary History of the United States, 1867–1960 (1963)
